There is a lot of debate about whether to use context compaction aggressively.



They show that with frequent compaction, frontier language models lose little to no accuracy on a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks while keeping their context short.



With one action per context, Claude Opus 4.5 scores 70.2 on SWE-bench Verified against 70.0 with the full history. Median peak context drops from 32K to 8K tokens.



The agent carries a short summary of its state between steps instead of the whole transcript. Simple compaction at the end of a conversation often does better than the full history, and Opus goes from 70.0 to 74.8 with it.



This also matters for cost. Later tokens cost more to generate than earlier ones, up to 7x on frontier open-weight models.



The pattern holds on Terminal-Bench, FRAMES, BFCLv3 and multilingual SWE-bench, with modest losses in some settings.



Before paying for million-token agent runs, it's worth testing aggressive compaction on your own tasks.

Yann LeCun was right & nobody in this industry wants to say it out loud.



109 million parameters beat 72 billion.



He has spent years saying scale is not the thing that makes a model understand the world. Meta bet the other way. He left in November and started his own lab in Paris.



Last Thursday he published the proof.



The theory everyone has been running on since 2024 is that if you train models big enough, on text, on images, on sound, they all end up with the same picture of reality inside them. Size does it. Nobody ever proved that part.



Randall Balestriero and LeCun proved it. And the proof says size was never doing the work.



What does the work is which two things you show a model together.



A photo and the caption of that photo are two views of one thing. Models trained on pairs like that get there fast.



Two paragraphs pulled from the same document are not two views of one thing. Models trained on those get there slowly and expensively.



Next word prediction is the second kind. That is what every chatbot in the world runs on.



In their tests the first method reached the same understanding after 21.6 million examples. Next word prediction needed 900 million.



And a 109 million parameter text model ended up closer to an image model's view of the world than a 72 billion parameter language model was.



660 times smaller.

I'm now building an "improvements" feature into all of my personal vibecoded applications: a freeform text input that's hooked up to an agent that yolo implements whatever is submitted.



It's an interesting experience -- the activation energy barrier to sanding any rough edge or implementing any new feature becomes extremely low. Someone else who uses one of the applications I created has already implemented 150 improvements over the course of a few days. This pattern feels like a new kind of tool -- liquid software? -- and every application that doesn't have this feature now has a slightly rigid and anachronistic flavor. Why can't I just tell it how I want it to be different?



Now, it's not obvious to me how this pattern can or should scale. Does it become unmaintainable after a while? (Maybe model intelligence improvement outstrips my feature appetite such that it's fine?) How does collaborative software work in this model? Can software designed this way be secure and reliable?



Whatever the larger questions about broader deployment, it definitely works great in a personal context. It reminds me a little of the visions of Lisp/Lisp machines, Smalltalk, and HyperCard -- systems that the user can take control of and modify. Those visions never quite worked, though: the vast majority of software today is not end-user modifiable in any useful way. So, while this "liquid" affordance is a very small touch, the way it changes one's relation to the software feels a bit transgressive and empowering in a Lickliderian and Engelbartian way.

🤖 Is AI really as objective as we think?



We often assume artificial intelligence provides neutral, fact-based answers. But what happens when AI inherits the biases hidden within the data it learns from? 🧠



AI bias is one of the biggest challenges facing the responsible use of artificial intelligence.



From recruitment and financial decisions to healthcare, business strategy and everyday research, biased AI outputs can reinforce stereotypes, overlook important perspectives and influence decisions in ways we might not even realise.



The solution isn't simply to stop using AI. It's to learn how to challenge it.



✅ Question the assumptions behind AI-generated answers.



✅ Ask for alternative perspectives and opposing arguments.



✅ Look for missing information and potential biases.



✅ Verify important claims against reliable sources.



Most importantly, don't confuse a confident AI response with an unbiased or accurate one.



AI should help us think more critically, not replace our critical thinking. 🚀

Anthropic (@AnthropicAI)



We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.



Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.



With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.



Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.



For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.



In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. The address examined five interconnected disciplines in Kautilya's framework. These include self-discipline of the office-holder, the responsibility of the State to enable people's well-being while protecting people’s existing livelihood, the use of independent information and diverse counsel in decision-making, institutional safeguards against misuse of public resources, and the interdependence of the different components of the State. Together, they offer an understanding of administration that encompasses individual conduct, sound institutional processes and the wider social and economic conditions in which governance operates.



The discussion also drew a connection between Kautilya's concept of Vinaya, or the continuous formation and discipline of a public servant, and the contemporary transition towards a role-based civil service. It brought attention to an important dimension of civil-service capacity, where professional competencies are accompanied by sound judgement, ethical conduct and an understanding of the purpose behind one's responsibilities. All of us understand that useful software is getting easier to create. But generating code, completing end-to-end engineering work, and creating business value are moving at very different rates. 



Digging into this from different angles. Epoch, for example, estimates that a fixed level of AI performance is getting cheaper 13x per year for the past 4 years. That's across math, science, and game projects. 



Anthropic's 100k C compiler experiment is well known: 20k API spend, roughly $200 per kLOC of code, but the compiler had major limitations, lots of bugs, and wasn't really comparable to a fully functional C compiler. 



An early 2026 Microsoft study estimates 25% more merged pull requests. Anthropic has shared bigger stats with us. What's not clear, though, is whether this translated into business value. It's an observational study, and in general, I am skeptical of observational data about increased activity.



A more recent September 2026 paper has impressive stats: 240%+ more commits, 80% more projects, 30% more releases, but it's output gains, not cost reductions. 



It's clear that cheaper software creation is going to make previously uneconomical software worth building: bespoke tools, small markets. I built a bunch of app & skills I would never have bothered to write actual code for before, for example. why? because it's cheap and easy.



Estimating value for these can be tricky. If, for example, somebody never created a piece of software that could create 10k of value because software costs 50k to create, and all of a sudden that 50k became 1k, the total economic value that's created is 9k, not 49k. This kind of "more is more" can be tricky to measure in terms of actual gain, either for a company or for society. 



The one other thing that people don't seem to keep in mind is that AI created software (all software?) comes with a poison pill: catastrophic bugs. 



If our ability to create new software grows out of proportion with our ability to detect them or, worse, fix them, we end up in a crisis-driven world. 



The world of crypto offers a warning here: there's a mind-numbing repetition of bugs with massive impact. Think about that. Would you tolerate that from your bank? 



Thinking about this as well as value capture from other world-changing inventions. Comment with ideas and thoughts.

Top 5 learnings growing The Rundown to 3.5M total active subscribers and 55%+ open rate:



1. Email is its own platform, treat it like YouTube, Instagram, Twitter



Super readers (open every email, click ads, and stick around for years) genuinely like email as a medium. We have millions of readers who don’t use social media. Best way to acquire them is through other newsletters, referrals, or being the reason they stop using social media.



Barely anyone is building for this audience. I’m more bullish on email than any other platform (long-form YouTube is a close second).



2. The newsletter industry lacks innovation



Look at mobile apps, ecom, edtech. Custom quiz onboarding, a landing page for every ad, hundreds of new creatives a day. Meanwhile most newsletters, including some of the biggest in the world, have a basic landing page and standard onboarding.



We built an onboarding quiz funnel that, at one point, got us close to negative CAC with hundreds of thousands a month in ad spend. That’s what let us scale aggressively and outbid competitors.



With AI coding and platforms like beehiiv, there’s no excuse not to build new experiences for your readers. The opportunity here is wide open :)



3. Newsletter sales is mostly an education problem



We still run social partnerships at a significantly higher CPM than our newsletters, yet the newsletters convert better and get way more clicks.



A lot of advertisers don’t understand newsletters as they do with influencer marketing, so at scale it becomes an education game. 



Once advertisers get it, they stay. We’ve been booked out at multiple ads a day for the last 3 years, months in advance.



4. Stay lean, fast, aggressive



Other newsletters have built large sales and content teams. I think it’s better to stay small and pay high-quality people to do very good work.



Revenue can increase with more employees, but the opportunity cost of not moving fast in the AI era is a long-term net negative. 



For example, we constantly test new growth experiments and new forms of media. Most don’t work and that’s fine. The point is we can pivot the same day because we're lean.



5. Lastly, don’t listen to people who say email is dead or that you shouldn’t run paid ads. That’s ignorance and lowkey skill issue.

Anthropic might even jump straight to Fable 6, just as it did with the unexpected version jump when Fable 5 was released



As for Astra, I doubt it'll be the biggest model in the GPT lineup. OpenAI clearly has something more powerful up its sleeve. My guess is GPT-7 Bel



The end of 2026 will mark the beginning of a transition to an entirely new generation of models



But this is pure speculation



2. 2027 will be the year of radical architectural experimentation



Transformers, at least in their classical form, will gradually give way to more efficient architectural components.



Several major AI labs have already made significant progress in exploring alternatives. The most promising directions include Mamba, Test-Time Training (TTT), and diffusion-based approaches to token generation.



I expect OpenAI and Anthropic to introduce entirely new experimental model families based on this research. They might not even carry the GPT or Claude branding



3. We're going to witness the return of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which were largely abandoned for years



Promising architectures like RWKV have already demonstrated that modern recurrent approaches have serious potential. In theory, they could also improve training efficiency and quality



4. There will be no RSI miracle.



Recursive self-improvement is a powerful way to automate routine research and engineering tasks, but it still depends on fundamental breakthroughs discovered and implemented by human researchers



And the worse your initial training and RL pipelines are, the greater the risk of regression from recursive synthetic training



It's a similar problem to what we see with distillation



5. New architectures will dramatically reduce the memory requirements of LLMs



Context windows will expand severalfold, while token generation speeds will increase significantly



In 2027, I expect models with context windows of 10 million tokens or more to become increasingly common



6. Haiku- and Luna-tier models will be discontinued



7. We'll see the emergence of highly efficient models with effectively unlimited usage.



It's entirely possible that Anthropic and OpenAI will release models with Opus 5.5-level capabilities that are no longer constrained by weekly usage limits



8. New architectures will revolutionize ultra-small local models capable of running directly on pocket-sized devices.



Major AI labs will develop incredibly efficient on-device models, but instead of releasing them openly, they'll distribute them under restrictive proprietary licenses to a small number of strategic partners, such as Apple, Sony, and others



9. Large open-weight models will fall significantly further behind the closed-source frontier.



Running the most capable open-weight models will still require hardware costing tens of thousands of dollars.



10. DeepSeek will pull even further ahead of its Chinese competitors in 2027



Meanwhile, China's broader AI industry will experience a major downturn. Many labs may shut down or face significant investment cuts as their economic inefficiencies become increasingly apparent



11. Many people predict that the memory and semiconductor shortage will become even worse next year



I'm more optimistic



By mid-2027, I expect a substantial decline in hardware prices and a significant improvement in component availability



12. Google will not win the AI race



Its stock will continue to fall, potentially much further



13. Apple stock will collapse



The company will fail to meaningfully adapt its devices and services to the AI era



Meanwhile, entirely new devices will emerge from smaller, lesser-known companies and AI labs, gradually erasing the boundaries between smartphones, laptops, and servers



Everything will be controlled through a single device, with a substantial portion of the computation happening in the cloud



14. Standalone apps and websites will gradually begin to disappear



Instead of navigating predefined interfaces, users will interact with software generated dynamically in real time for their specific needs



Code itself will cease to be the primary source of value



We're already seeing the first signs of this with ChatGPT and Claude generating interactive widgets directly in their responses. This trend will accelerate dramatically



15. We're about to witness a renaissance in game development



Years of creative stagnation, repetitive formulas, and absurdly bloated development budgets will finally come to an end



Within the next two years, game development costs and production timelines will be cut in half



More and more solo developers will start releasing games with AA+ production quality



Many major publishers will enter a severe crisis. Their stock prices could collapse severalfold



16. 2027 will be the most devastating year for the stock market in human history



We'll witness the decline of an enormous number of corporations that have seemed untouchable for decades



17. Early human trials of a new generation of cancer treatments will demonstrate cure rates approaching 90%



By 2029, these groundbreaking treatments will become widely available

People assume that in an AI doing formal verification world, they can take their existing codebase, ask AI to prove it correct, and get either a proof or a bug.



Sadly reality has a few bones to pick with this, and one of them is the "existing codebase" part. And that's due to the good ol' halting problem.



The short of it is that there is no general purpose algorithm that takes any program and input and correctly determines whether it will terminate or run forever. With a few mathematical flourishes we can extend that to "Rice's theorem" and prove this is true for any nontrivial semantic property, meaning we can't automatically prove arbitrary things about arbitrary programs.



Now obviously we can prove some things about some programs, or else formal verification wouldn't exist as a field. The trick is that we write the code in a style suitable for verification. One example of this is totality: in Lean, all functions must be guaranteed to return a value for all inputs. If we want some code that runs forever (like f.ex a server), instead of `while true` we do `while (i < 10^60)` so that it's guaranteed to terminate and return a value (after the end of the universe).



(Totality is also why, in Lean, `1/0 == 0`. If you convert your code to Lean without accounting for this, you could have correct lean but incorrect code!)



Another "style" we use is state machines. Even if your code doesn't quite fit an SM architecture, if you want to prove it at scale, you're probably going to go with a state machine. State machines are the carcinisation of provable code.



Hopefully by now the problem is clearer: even if your codebase is objectively correct, it might not be in the right shape to be proven correct!



Okay, just have the AI rewrite your codebase into another form, right? Two problems. One: you don't know if you've introduced errors in the rewrite because you can't prove them equivalent (since one of them is not in a provable shape). Two: making code more verifiable can make it worse on other metrics, like modifiability, performance, and complexity. And now you've got the old bugbear of software engineers, the dreaded tradeoff.



Now, don't get me wrong, formal verification has a huge role in the future of software, but it's not going to be a breezy "prove my Ruby thx" Claude prompt. It's still going to take work and expertise on our parts to prove our code, and to strike the right balance between formal verification and other forms of correctness.



This is one reason I'm so excited to be working at @AntithesisHQ , which tackles a lot of the same properties as proof methods, but verifies them with "deterministic simulation testing" and fuzzing instead of with a proofs. So it's not as thorough and doesn't give you confidence in all inputs, but it automatically works on pretty much any code shape. I've literally grabbed open source projects off Github, told Claude "check properties XYZ in Antithesis thx", and gotten bug reports back. No state machine rewrites needed.

AI is writing more of your code. But can you trust it?

We make high-resolution 3D wind predictions in seconds to guide energy-efficient drone planning.



Wind-aware planners often assume the wind field is already known. But simulating airflow around buildings takes hours of CFD, making it impractical for short drone missions when wind conditions change.



Our approach couples wind prediction with trajectory optimization. By rotating the city layout to align with a fixed reference wind, we turn wind-direction generalization into building-geometry generalization. A localized neural operator uses multi-directional distance features to predict 3D wind within a flight corridor. The planner then optimizes the drone’s path and speed in continuous 3D space to reduce energy use. In our simulations, the drone generally flies higher and faster in tailwinds, lower and slower in headwinds, and shifts sideways to exploit favorable local winds.



Corridor prediction takes about 3 seconds versus roughly 8 hours for full-domain CFD. Compared with wind-agnostic planning, our method reduces average energy use per kilometer by 12.7% in headwinds, 6.9% in tailwinds, and 4.5% in crosswinds in CFD-evaluated simulations. It captures 75–88% of the energy savings achieved with CFD-reference wind fields.



Moving forward, we will focus on turning AI predictions of the physical world into actionable decisions for autonomous systems. Follow our lab for updates: dual.xiongyexiao.com

In his address, Prof. Das underlined the need for a coordinated approach to disease control, bringing together prevention, early detection and public health awareness to address both communicable diseases and the growing burden of non-communicable diseases.
